fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Benchmark cause of slowness in Displayed.Instances.Sets.Properties

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Build standalone Agda programs that measure typechecking time as a function of reindexing depth and proof style, to confirm or falsify the hypothesis that the slowness in Displayed.Instances.Sets.Properties comes from nested reindexings combined with filler-at-a-time proofs (many transports over refl).

Constraint: do not edit the library. The benchmarks should be contrived client programs that import existing library code and exercise the suspected-pathological patterns at controlled depth, so the measurement is attributable to a specific shape rather than the library as a whole. Compare against the hcomp-en-masse alternative from the hcomp speedup note.

Output: a short writeup of which patterns are linear-vs-superlinear in depth and which are not, sufficient to decide whether Yoneda strictification actually attacks the right cost. This decision gates the broader strictification experiments outlined in the 2026-05-05 meeting notes.
Background: the original slowness observation and the hcomp-based workaround. Subtask of the Logical Relations on Display milestone.
Bench files live at Bench/ReindFillerChains/. The driver is run-bench.sh; REPS=3 ./run-bench.sh reduces variance.

html:ul.html:li: Flat (Implicit/Explicit{01..32}.agda): Postulated Z, X : Type, pt : Z → X, q : (z : Z) → Yᴰ (pt z), with mp = refl ∙∙ refl ∙∙ refl and a chain rectifyOut $ reind-filler⁻ _ ∙ ... ∙ reind-filler⁻ _ of length n. The Explicit variants fill {a, b, p} on every reind-filler⁻.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The Real family reproduces the slowness from Sets/Properties.agda. Three findings:

html:ol.html:li: Apparent step function at depth 4 is "first successful elaboration", not a unifier threshold: Real01–Real03 fail fast with a type-mismatch error because the chain is too short for endpoints to unify (see Open Questions). Depth 4 is the minimum chain length that elaborates at all, after which post-typing work fires. Past depth 4 the cost plateaus (~30ms per added junction through depth 64), so the chain length itself is not the expensive part.

Lossy-unification dominates: removing --lossy-unification turns the depth-4 case from ~13s into 213s — a 16× blowup. The flat ∙-chain over real SETᴰ.Hom[_][_,_] types is what lossy bounds; without it the unifier does real work on every junction trying to normalize the deeply-nested fiber types.

Postulated types don't trigger this: Wrapped04 (same shape, postulated types, refl-equivalent mp) is fast — the unifier blowup is type-driven. The cost is in unifying SETᴰ hom-types — concretely Hom[ Z , X ][ Zᴰ , g*Xᴰ ] where g*Xᴰ unfolds through isFibrationSETᴰ._*_, presheaf reindexing, LRⱽObᴰ→LRⱽ, etc. — not in unifying reind-filler⁻ implicits over a postulated P : (Z → X) → Type.

fr:title.text: What the bookkeeping is over: unsolved metas, not an elaborated term

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: What the bookkeeping is over: unsolved metas, not an elaborated term

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Removing --allow-unsolved-metas from Real04 fails with [UnsolvedConstraints]. Same for RealFlat04. So with --lossy-unification on, Agda doesn't actually finish elaborating the proof. The body persisted to the interface is a single reference to an unsolved meta (unsolvedmeta.N) parameterised by the module's level args. The "elaborated term" I attributed the cost to in earlier drafts of this tree doesn't exist.

What does exist in the meta-store: 384 unsolved metas for Real04, 174 for RealFlat04, 73 for Real00. Each unsolved meta carries a type, a context (telescope of variables in scope), and entries on Agda's constraint list. With lossy on, Agda gives up on the trickier ones rather than recursing forever, and they remain in the store. The 11.5s of bookkeeping is over those 384 meta entries, each of which has a SETᴰ.Hom[_][_,_]-flavoured type that mentions g*Xᴰ = isFibrationSETᴰ._*_ g Xᴰ, the cartesian-product-fibration combinator, LRⱽObᴰ→LRⱽ, etc.
Direct AST measurements on the postulated-type fixtures (which DO fully elaborate, no unsolved metas) — by reflection in Bench/ReindFillerChains/SizeReflect.agda:
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: GOAL ELABORATED AST NODES AGDA WALL TIME Implicit01 55 0.87s Implicit04 688 0.90s Implicit16 8,350 0.86s Implicit32 31,334 0.87s Wrapped01 688 0.97s Wrapped04 1,507 0.98s
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Two things stand out. First, on postulated types, term size grows quadratically with chain depth — 31k nodes at depth 32. Second, none of that matters for time: those cases all check in under 1s, dominated by interface-deserialization. So size alone is not the cost driver.

The cost driver is the meta store, not the elaborated term. Each Implicit/Wrapped AST node is R.def (quote postulate) — trivial for downstream passes to look up, highlight, serialize, and the postulated fixtures fully elaborate so no metas are left behind. In the real SETᴰ setting, the analogous pieces reference deep qualified names inside the displayed-presheaf infrastructure, the unifier under lossy gives up rather than recursing, and 384 entries remain in the meta store. The cost decomposes as
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: cost ≈ (meta count) × (per-meta type complexity) × (unifier work per call)
fr:mainmatter.html:p: where the "unifier work per call" factor is what --lossy-unification bounds at typing time, and the bookkeeping passes (InverseNameLookup, Highlighting, Serialization, Miscellaneous) walk the remaining (\text {meta count}) \times (\text {per-meta type complexity}) entries post-typing. Each lever attacks a different factor and they compose multiplicatively — see the annotation experiment below for the quantitative split.

The plateau on depth (Real04=13.0s, Real16=13.4s, Real32=14.1s, Real64=14.8s — ~30ms per junction past 4) is consistent: each extra junction adds one meta with similar type complexity, so the per-junction cost is small relative to the fixed cost of the wrapping itself.

fr:title.text: Why displayed presheaves are catastrophically worse

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Why displayed presheaves are catastrophically worse

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The same wrapping pattern, applied to displayed presheaves, has each junction's Hom-type be a NatTrans (component functions + naturality). Per-meta type complexity is multiplicatively bigger. Bookkeeping cost is (\text {meta count}) \times (\text {per-meta type complexity}), so the displayed-presheaf case scales worse along the type-complexity axis even at the same chain depth.

The comment in Sets/Properties.agda hypothesised that the slowness comes from "the unification of the implicit arguments to each of these reind fillers… we may mitigate the slowness here by removing nested reindexings." Sharper picture now:

html:ul.html:li: Right that unification is implicated and type-driven. 213s without --lossy-unification on the depth-4 chain; postulated-type fixtures (Wrapped, Implicit, Explicit) cannot reproduce the slowness even at depth 32 (31,334 AST nodes), so the cost is in unifying real SETᴰ.Hom[_][_,_] types, not in the chain shape itself.

Right that filling implicits helps — but the path argument, not the type implicits. Filling {a, b, p} on every reind-filler⁻ (the Explicit fixture) doesn't move the postulated case, which was already fast. But replacing the e : a ≡ b path argument with refl on the real chain gives a 2× speedup (13.13s → 6.20s on the bench, 14.83s → 6.75s in the actual library) by short-circuiting the unifier search at each reind-filler⁻ call.

Wrong about "nested reindexings" being the lever. Cutting nesting depth only saves ~30ms per junction past depth 4 — Real04≈Real16 ≈Real64 under lossy. The proof shape's chain length is not what's expensive.

The dominant residual cost is bookkeeping over the meta store. With lossy on, typing is 1.3 percent of the total; the remaining 11.5s is post-typing work over 384 unsolved metas, set by (\text {meta count}) \times (\text {per-meta type complexity}). Lossy and explicit-refl attack the typing factor; strictification is what attacks per-meta type complexity (and shrinks the bookkeeping bill proportionally).

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Yoneda strictification is still the right fix, with a sharper reason than the original comment suggested. The win is not "the unifier sees fewer reduction obligations". The win is "each unsolved meta in the store has a smaller, simpler type", because the strictified fiber types substituted into each junction are smaller. The downstream bookkeeping passes (scope lookup, highlighting, interface build) walk those meta types and shrink proportionally.

Concrete prediction: strictification should drop Real04 from ~13s back toward Real00's ~3.4s import baseline, mostly by collapsing the Miscellaneous + InverseNameLookup + Highlighting + Serialization buckets, not the Typing bucket (which is already small under lossy).

It will not eliminate the import cost (Real00 is 3.4s with the current import graph, almost entirely in deserialization) — that's a separate concern about the size of the displayed-presheaf infrastructure being pulled in.

It does not obviate --lossy-unification: removing lossy turns the depth-4 case into 213s. The three levers attack different factors of (meta count) × (per-meta type complexity) × (unifier work per call) and are independent:

html:ul.html:li: --lossy-unification bounds unifier work per call (16×).
_ → refl annotation further cuts unifier work per call on top of lossy (2× more).
Strictification shrinks per-meta type complexity, which feeds through to both the typing cost and the post-typing bookkeeping.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: All three should be applied together. Strictification is the most invasive but addresses the largest single multiplier and the only one that touches the bookkeeping bill.

fr:title.text: Annotation experiment: explicit refl gives 2× on top of lossy

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Annotation experiment: explicit refl gives 2× on top of lossy

fr:mainmatter.html:p: User hypothesis: "many unification problems with dependencies, where later problems depend on earlier ones; filling sufficient annotations should disambiguate and give a big speedup." Tested by replacing each _ argument to reind-filler⁻ with refl.
Bench fixture: Bench/ReindFillerChains/Real04AllRefl.agda. Wall times under --lossy-unification --allow-unsolved-metas:
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: Real04 baseline (`_` × 6, lossy) 13.13 s 384 metas Real04AllRefl (refl × 6, lossy) 6.20 s 389 metas Real04 baseline (`_` × 6, NO lossy) 213 s -- Real04AllRefl (refl × 6, NO lossy) 203.82 s --
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Confirmed in the actual library by uncommenting ExponentialsⱽSETᴰueⱽ in Cubical/Categories/Displayed/Instances/Sets/Properties.agda (.snd.snd left as a hole, matching the pre-existing comment) and toggling the same _ ↔ refl change:
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: Properties.agda (Exp commented out) 3.79 s Properties.agda (Exp live, `_` × 6) 14.83 s Properties.agda (Exp live, refl × 6) 6.75 s
fr:mainmatter.html:p: 2.18× speedup in the real file. The bench was faithful — the same change that worked on the contrived bench works on the actual definition. Caveat: the _s in isFibrationSETᴰueⱽ and BinProductsⱽSETᴰueⱽ do not accept refl (those fillers produce non-trivial paths, unlike the rectifyOut/congᴰ-wrapped chain inside Exp). The intervention is specific to wrapped reindexing chains.

html:ul.html:li: Lossy attacks per-meta type complexity. It bounds how much work the unifier does normalizing the huge SETᴰ.Hom[_][_,_] types attached to each meta.

Annotation attacks per-meta unifier work. Even after lossy makes each meta tractable, the unifier still spends real time searching for e : a ≡ b at each reind-filler⁻ call. Handing it refl short-circuits that search.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Meta count is essentially unchanged (384 → 389, basically noise). The user's hypothesis that "filling earlier metas resolves later ones" is not what's happening — invisible metas like _b_237, _a_276, _bᴰ.fst_358 survive both runs. Annotation reduces work per meta, not number of metas.
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: cost ≈ (meta count) × (per-meta type complexity) × (unifier work per call) ↑ ↑ ↑ (mostly fixed (lossy attacks (annotation attacks by proof shape) this; strictifi- this) cation also)
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Practical take: in real Properties.agda code, the easy mechanical intervention reind-filler⁻ _ → reind-filler⁻ refl (where applicable) should give about a 2× speedup. It does not obviate --lossy-unification or strictification — those still own the bigger factors.

This explains the user's prior empirical observation: running C-u C-u C-c C-s (Solve constraints at strongest normalization) on ? holes returns refl-shaped solutions that, when written back into the source, give exactly this 2× speedup. The investigation here just quantifies what that interactive workflow was achieving.

Caveat: writing refl only works because, in this specific proof shape, every e : a ≡ b arising from reind-filler⁻ reduces under the rectifyOut/congᴰ wrapping to a path of compositions that collapses to refl once the implicit fiber types are pinned. In a more general chain you might need a non-trivial composite — but in that case C-u C-u C-c C-s still gives the right thing.

Decision implication: strictification + lossy + explicit refl are the three independent levers. Strictification is the most invasive but addresses the largest factor (per-meta type complexity, multiplicatively shrinks meta sizes); the _→refl cleanup is a cheap mechanical 2× before doing any structural work.

html:ul.html:li: The depth 3→4 step (Real03 = 4.07s, Real04 = 12.97s) is now understood as "first successful elaboration", not a lossy threshold. Real01–Real03 fail fast with a type-mismatch error because the chain is too short for endpoints to unify. Depth 4 is the minimum chain length that elaborates at all, at which point the post-typing bookkeeping fires. Worth confirming by a typecheck-only benchmark that disables Highlighting and Serialization, if Agda exposes the knobs.

Does the refl-annotation lever transfer to the UniversalQuantifierⱽ proof shape? ExponentialsⱽSETᴰueⱽ benefits 2× because its rectifyOut/congᴰ-wrapped chain reduces to refl once implicits are pinned. The non-Eq UQ counterpart isn't written in the library yet (the legacy commented block in Sets/Properties.agda uses an obsolete API). When someone is already inside that file, attempting the construction is the cheapest way to find out.

Does the snd .snd field (currently a {!!} hole in ExponentialsⱽSETᴰueⱽ and in the bench files) have the same shape when filled? It would add another rectifyOut/congᴰ/funExt₂/ΣPathP block and (per the cost model) multiply the meta count again.

Is Scoping.InverseNameLookup actually triggered by typing-time pretty-printing of constraints, in which case it's partly typing cost masquerading as bookkeeping? Highlighting and Serialization (3.76s combined) are unambiguously post-typing; the Miscellaneous + InverseNameLookup attribution is fuzzier. The qualitative claim ("typing under lossy is a small slice, meta-store bookkeeping dominates") holds either way.

fr:title.text: Fibrations into a 1-category of groupoid-object categories

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Fibrations into a 1-category of groupoid-object categories

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Explore a streamlined setup for logical relations: work with a small category \mathcal {GC} whose objects are categories equipped with a groupoid object (or, equivalently, categories in which every map is invertible in the relevant sense), and whose morphisms are the appropriate structure-preserving functors. Define fibrations as functors into \mathcal {GC}. Because each fiber is a groupoid-enriched 1-category, \mathcal {GC} itself is a 1-category — there are no higher coherences to manage.

Motivation. The current displayed-category machinery in Finishing Logical Relations on Display spends a lot of effort on coherences that evaporate once the fibers are forced to be (truncated to) groupoidal. If the target 1-category is rich enough to express the constructions needed for canonicity and normalization logical relations, this may be a lighter foundation than the thickened / displayed-double-category route.

html:ol.html:li: Define the small 1-category \mathcal {GC} of categories-with-groupoid-objects and verify it is a 1-category (no higher cells).
Define fibrations as functors E \to \mathcal {GC} and relate them to the displayed-category presentation already in the library.
Encode the universal properties needed for semantics: terminal / binary products / exponentials at the base, plus their fiberwise analogues.
Encode universal quantification (right adjoint to pullback / reindexing) internally to this framework.
State and prove Beck--Chevalley for the relevant pullback squares.
State and prove Frobenius reciprocity for the left-adjoint / existential direction.
Reconstruct the canonicity logical relation in this framework as a first test case.
Reconstruct the normalization logical relation in this framework as a harder stress test.

html:ul.html:li: What exactly is the right notion of "groupoid object" here — an internal groupoid, a hom-groupoid enrichment, or truncation of hom-sets to sets? The choice affects whether \mathcal {GC} is genuinely small.
Does the 1-categorical structure survive once we add the universal-quantifier / Beck--Chevalley / Frobenius data, or do higher coherences creep back in through the adjoints?
How does this compare to the displayed-category-with-isos setup in Cubical/Categories/Displayed/ and the thickened displayed categories of PR 253?

The Real family reproduces the slowness from Sets/Properties.agda. Three findings:
Apparent step function at depth 4 is "first successful elaboration", not a unifier threshold: Real01–Real03 fail fast with a type-mismatch error because the chain is too short for endpoints to unify (see Open Questions). Depth 4 is the minimum chain length that elaborates at all, after which post-typing work fires. Past depth 4 the cost plateaus (~30ms per added junction through depth 64), so the chain length itself is not the expensive part.
Lossy-unification dominates: removing --lossy-unification turns the depth-4 case from ~13s into 213s — a 16× blowup. The flat ∙-chain over real SETᴰ.Hom[_][_,_] types is what lossy bounds; without it the unifier does real work on every junction trying to normalize the deeply-nested fiber types.
Postulated types don't trigger this: Wrapped04 (same shape, postulated types, refl-equivalent mp) is fast — the unifier blowup is type-driven. The cost is in unifying SETᴰ hom-types — concretely Hom[ Z , X ][ Zᴰ , g*Xᴰ ] where g*Xᴰ unfolds through isFibrationSETᴰ._*_, presheaf reindexing, LRⱽObᴰ→LRⱽ, etc. — not in unifying reind-filler⁻ implicits over a postulated P : (Z → X) → Type.Steven Schaefer202656/Users/stevenschaefer/forest/trees/sss-00BO.treeProfile breakdown
Where the time goes inside Agda, with --lossy-unification on. agda --profile=internal Real04.agda (cache warmed, only the bench file rechecked): Real04 Real00-noBody RealFlat04 Total 14,969ms 3,105ms 1,389ms Typing 193ms 2ms 6ms Typing.OccursCheck 186ms - - Typing.CheckRHS 60ms - - Scoping.InverseNameLookup 3,756ms - - Miscellaneous 3,723ms 26ms 27ms Deserialization 3,084ms 2,928ms 1,275ms Highlighting 2,464ms - - Serialization.BuildInterface 1,299ms - - metas 384 73 174
Typing share of total in Real04: 193 / 14,969 = 1.3 percent.
Real00 has no proof body and only imports Properties.agda (3.1s, of which 2.9s is interface deserialization — fixed cost, cache-driven). RealFlat04 has the depth-4 ∙-chain on real SETᴰ.Hom[_][_,_] types but no wrapping — no rectifyOut, no congᴰ, no funExt₂, no ΣPathP. It costs 1.39s.
So adding the wrapped proof body on top of the import skeleton spends:
~450ms on actual typing/unification under lossy (the ∙-chain over SETᴰ.Hom types — what --lossy-unification bounds, and what the _ → refl annotation further cuts).
~11.5s on post-typing bookkeeping: scope-name lookup, the Miscellaneous bucket, syntax highlighting, building the interface — driven by the size of the unsolved meta store.
Without --lossy-unification, the typing budget rises from ~450ms to ~210s and dominates everything else; lossy is doing essential work even though it doesn't show up as a big slice of the profile under the lossy run. The annotation experiment subtree below quantifies what's left of the typing budget after lossy and how to attack it further.Steven Schaefer202656/Users/stevenschaefer/forest/trees/sss-00BO.treeWhat the bookkeeping is over: unsolved metas, not an elaborated term
Removing --allow-unsolved-metas from Real04 fails with [UnsolvedConstraints]. Same for RealFlat04. So with --lossy-unification on, Agda doesn't actually finish elaborating the proof. The body persisted to the interface is a single reference to an unsolved meta (unsolvedmeta.N) parameterised by the module's level args. The "elaborated term" I attributed the cost to in earlier drafts of this tree doesn't exist.
What does exist in the meta-store: 384 unsolved metas for Real04, 174 for RealFlat04, 73 for Real00. Each unsolved meta carries a type, a context (telescope of variables in scope), and entries on Agda's constraint list. With lossy on, Agda gives up on the trickier ones rather than recursing forever, and they remain in the store. The 11.5s of bookkeeping is over those 384 meta entries, each of which has a SETᴰ.Hom[_][_,_]-flavoured type that mentions g*Xᴰ = isFibrationSETᴰ._*_ g Xᴰ, the cartesian-product-fibration combinator, LRⱽObᴰ→LRⱽ, etc.
Direct AST measurements on the postulated-type fixtures (which DO fully elaborate, no unsolved metas) — by reflection in Bench/ReindFillerChains/SizeReflect.agda: GOAL ELABORATED AST NODES AGDA WALL TIME Implicit01 55 0.87s Implicit04 688 0.90s Implicit16 8,350 0.86s Implicit32 31,334 0.87s Wrapped01 688 0.97s Wrapped04 1,507 0.98s
Two things stand out. First, on postulated types, term size grows quadratically with chain depth — 31k nodes at depth 32. Second, none of that matters for time: those cases all check in under 1s, dominated by interface-deserialization. So size alone is not the cost driver.
The cost driver is the meta store, not the elaborated term. Each Implicit/Wrapped AST node is R.def (quote postulate) — trivial for downstream passes to look up, highlight, serialize, and the postulated fixtures fully elaborate so no metas are left behind. In the real SETᴰ setting, the analogous pieces reference deep qualified names inside the displayed-presheaf infrastructure, the unifier under lossy gives up rather than recursing, and 384 entries remain in the meta store. The cost decomposes as cost ≈ (meta count) × (per-meta type complexity) × (unifier work per call)
where the "unifier work per call" factor is what --lossy-unification bounds at typing time, and the bookkeeping passes (InverseNameLookup, Highlighting, Serialization, Miscellaneous) walk the remaining (\text {meta count}) \times (\text {per-meta type complexity}) entries post-typing. Each lever attacks a different factor and they compose multiplicatively — see the annotation experiment below for the quantitative split.
The plateau on depth (Real04=13.0s, Real16=13.4s, Real32=14.1s, Real64=14.8s — ~30ms per junction past 4) is consistent: each extra junction adds one meta with similar type complexity, so the per-junction cost is small relative to the fixed cost of the wrapping itself.Steven Schaefer202656/Users/stevenschaefer/forest/trees/sss-00BO.treeWhy displayed presheaves are catastrophically worse
The same wrapping pattern, applied to displayed presheaves, has each junction's Hom-type be a NatTrans (component functions + naturality). Per-meta type complexity is multiplicatively bigger. Bookkeeping cost is (\text {meta count}) \times (\text {per-meta type complexity}), so the displayed-presheaf case scales worse along the type-complexity axis even at the same chain depth.Steven Schaefer202656/Users/stevenschaefer/forest/trees/sss-00BO.treeVerdict on the original hypothesis
The comment in Sets/Properties.agda hypothesised that the slowness comes from "the unification of the implicit arguments to each of these reind fillers… we may mitigate the slowness here by removing nested reindexings." Sharper picture now:
Right that unification is implicated and type-driven. 213s without --lossy-unification on the depth-4 chain; postulated-type fixtures (Wrapped, Implicit, Explicit) cannot reproduce the slowness even at depth 32 (31,334 AST nodes), so the cost is in unifying real SETᴰ.Hom[_][_,_] types, not in the chain shape itself.
Right that filling implicits helps — but the path argument, not the type implicits. Filling {a, b, p} on every reind-filler⁻ (the Explicit fixture) doesn't move the postulated case, which was already fast. But replacing the e : a ≡ b path argument with refl on the real chain gives a 2× speedup (13.13s → 6.20s on the bench, 14.83s → 6.75s in the actual library) by short-circuiting the unifier search at each reind-filler⁻ call.
Wrong about "nested reindexings" being the lever. Cutting nesting depth only saves ~30ms per junction past depth 4 — Real04≈Real16 ≈Real64 under lossy. The proof shape's chain length is not what's expensive.
The dominant residual cost is bookkeeping over the meta store. With lossy on, typing is 1.3 percent of the total; the remaining 11.5s is post-typing work over 384 unsolved metas, set by (\text {meta count}) \times (\text {per-meta type complexity}). Lossy and explicit-refl attack the typing factor; strictification is what attacks per-meta type complexity (and shrinks the bookkeeping bill proportionally).Steven Schaefer202656/Users/stevenschaefer/forest/trees/sss-00BO.treeDecision on Yoneda strictification
Yoneda strictification is still the right fix, with a sharper reason than the original comment suggested. The win is not "the unifier sees fewer reduction obligations". The win is "each unsolved meta in the store has a smaller, simpler type", because the strictified fiber types substituted into each junction are smaller. The downstream bookkeeping passes (scope lookup, highlighting, interface build) walk those meta types and shrink proportionally.
Concrete prediction: strictification should drop Real04 from ~13s back toward Real00's ~3.4s import baseline, mostly by collapsing the Miscellaneous + InverseNameLookup + Highlighting + Serialization buckets, not the Typing bucket (which is already small under lossy).
It will not eliminate the import cost (Real00 is 3.4s with the current import graph, almost entirely in deserialization) — that's a separate concern about the size of the displayed-presheaf infrastructure being pulled in.
It does not obviate --lossy-unification: removing lossy turns the depth-4 case into 213s. The three levers attack different factors of (meta count) × (per-meta type complexity) × (unifier work per call) and are independent:
--lossy-unification bounds unifier work per call (16×).
_ → refl annotation further cuts unifier work per call on top of lossy (2× more).
Strictification shrinks per-meta type complexity, which feeds through to both the typing cost and the post-typing bookkeeping.
All three should be applied together. Strictification is the most invasive but addresses the largest single multiplier and the only one that touches the bookkeeping bill.Steven Schaefer202656/Users/stevenschaefer/forest/trees/sss-00BO.treeAnnotation experiment: explicit refl gives 2× on top of lossy
User hypothesis: "many unification problems with dependencies, where later problems depend on earlier ones; filling sufficient annotations should disambiguate and give a big speedup." Tested by replacing each _ argument to reind-filler⁻ with refl.
Bench fixture: Bench/ReindFillerChains/Real04AllRefl.agda. Wall times under --lossy-unification --allow-unsolved-metas: Real04 baseline (`_` × 6, lossy) 13.13 s 384 metas Real04AllRefl (refl × 6, lossy) 6.20 s 389 metas Real04 baseline (`_` × 6, NO lossy) 213 s -- Real04AllRefl (refl × 6, NO lossy) 203.82 s --
Confirmed in the actual library by uncommenting ExponentialsⱽSETᴰueⱽ in Cubical/Categories/Displayed/Instances/Sets/Properties.agda (.snd.snd left as a hole, matching the pre-existing comment) and toggling the same _ ↔ refl change: Properties.agda (Exp commented out) 3.79 s Properties.agda (Exp live, `_` × 6) 14.83 s Properties.agda (Exp live, refl × 6) 6.75 s
2.18× speedup in the real file. The bench was faithful — the same change that worked on the contrived bench works on the actual definition. Caveat: the _s in isFibrationSETᴰueⱽ and BinProductsⱽSETᴰueⱽ do not accept refl (those fillers produce non-trivial paths, unlike the rectifyOut/congᴰ-wrapped chain inside Exp). The intervention is specific to wrapped reindexing chains.
Two independent factors. Lossy unification gives 16× (213→13s); explicit refl on top of lossy gives an additional 2× (13→6.2s). With lossy off, refl buys only ~5 percent. So:
Lossy attacks per-meta type complexity. It bounds how much work the unifier does normalizing the huge SETᴰ.Hom[_][_,_] types attached to each meta.
Annotation attacks per-meta unifier work. Even after lossy makes each meta tractable, the unifier still spends real time searching for e : a ≡ b at each reind-filler⁻ call. Handing it refl short-circuits that search.
Meta count is essentially unchanged (384 → 389, basically noise). The user's hypothesis that "filling earlier metas resolves later ones" is not what's happening — invisible metas like _b_237, _a_276, _bᴰ.fst_358 survive both runs. Annotation reduces work per meta, not number of metas.
Refined cost model: cost ≈ (meta count) × (per-meta type complexity) × (unifier work per call) ↑ ↑ ↑ (mostly fixed (lossy attacks (annotation attacks by proof shape) this; strictifi- this) cation also)
Practical take: in real Properties.agda code, the easy mechanical intervention reind-filler⁻ _ → reind-filler⁻ refl (where applicable) should give about a 2× speedup. It does not obviate --lossy-unification or strictification — those still own the bigger factors.
This explains the user's prior empirical observation: running C-u C-u C-c C-s (Solve constraints at strongest normalization) on ? holes returns refl-shaped solutions that, when written back into the source, give exactly this 2× speedup. The investigation here just quantifies what that interactive workflow was achieving.
Caveat: writing refl only works because, in this specific proof shape, every e : a ≡ b arising from reind-filler⁻ reduces under the rectifyOut/congᴰ wrapping to a path of compositions that collapses to refl once the implicit fiber types are pinned. In a more general chain you might need a non-trivial composite — but in that case C-u C-u C-c C-s still gives the right thing.
Decision implication: strictification + lossy + explicit refl are the three independent levers. Strictification is the most invasive but addresses the largest factor (per-meta type complexity, multiplicatively shrinks meta sizes); the _→refl cleanup is a cheap mechanical 2× before doing any structural work.Steven Schaefer202656/Users/stevenschaefer/forest/trees/sss-00BO.treeOpen questions

The qualitative claim ("typing under lossy is a small slice, meta-store bookkeeping dominates") holds either way.Steven Schaefer2026424/Users/stevenschaefer/forest/trees/sss-00B5.treehttps://stevenschaefer.net/sss-00B5/sss-00B5/sss-00B5/Fibrations into a 1-category of groupoid-object categoriesTODOcancelledmedium
Explore a streamlined setup for logical relations: work with a small category \mathcal {GC} whose objects are categories equipped with a groupoid object (or, equivalently, categories in which every map is invertible in the relevant sense), and whose morphisms are the appropriate structure-preserving functors. Define fibrations as functors into \mathcal {GC}. Because each fiber is a groupoid-enriched 1-category, \mathcal {GC} itself is a 1-category — there are no higher coherences to manage.
Motivation. The current displayed-category machinery in Finishing Logical Relations on Display spends a lot of effort on coherences that evaporate once the fibers are forced to be (truncated to) groupoidal. If the target 1-category is rich enough to express the constructions needed for canonicity and normalization logical relations, this may be a lighter foundation than the thickened / displayed-double-category route.
Deliverables.
Define the small 1-category \mathcal {GC} of categories-with-groupoid-objects and verify it is a 1-category (no higher cells).
Define fibrations as functors E \to \mathcal {GC} and relate them to the displayed-category presentation already in the library.
Encode the universal properties needed for semantics: terminal / binary products / exponentials at the base, plus their fiberwise analogues.
Encode universal quantification (right adjoint to pullback / reindexing) internally to this framework.
State and prove Beck--Chevalley for the relevant pullback squares.
State and prove Frobenius reciprocity for the left-adjoint / existential direction.
Reconstruct the canonicity logical relation in this framework as a first test case.
Reconstruct the normalization logical relation in this framework as a harder stress test.
Open questions.
What exactly is the right notion of "groupoid object" here — an internal groupoid, a hom-groupoid enrichment, or truncation of hom-sets to sets? The choice affects whether \mathcal {GC} is genuinely small.
Does the 1-categorical structure survive once we add the universal-quantifier / Beck--Chevalley / Frobenius data, or do higher coherences creep back in through the adjoints?
How does this compare to the displayed-category-with-isos setup in Cubical/Categories/Displayed/ and the thickened displayed categories of PR 253?

fr:title.text: PhD roadmap: Dependent Lambek Calculus as the central object

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: PhD roadmap: Dependent Lambek Calculus as the central object

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Two-year sketch. Expansion of the PhD-roadmap section of the 2026-05-13 meeting prep, drafted for discussion with Max. Replaces the one-paragraph sketch there.

Thesis claim. Dependent Lambek Calculus (DLC) is the central object of the dissertation. DLC is developed along three coupled axes: categorical-semantic metatheory (via displayed categories), algorithmic content (compositional characterizations of practical parsing algorithms), and implementation (a Lean tool usable enough to host real-language parser correctness proofs). The synthesis chapter is self-hosted parser correctness for the Lean and Agda frontends, written inside the host languages themselves.

Why the three axes are one PhD, not three. The displayed-categorical machinery makes the parsing-theoretic content mechanizable; the parsing-theoretic content motivates and stress-tests the foundational machinery; the Lean implementation is what makes the correctness claims executable on real proof-assistant frontends. Strictification (Strictification) cuts across as the enabling technique for mechanization.

Paper 1: Logical Relations on Display. In flight; target submission in ~3 months. Establishes the displayed-categorical framework that downstream papers use to mechanize DLC metatheorems. Gated by the conservativity rewrite and the formalization-slowness fix; tracked at the paper milestone. The strictification technique (Yoneda Strictification: Tradeoffs and Opportunities, Fibrations into a 1-category of groupoid-object categories) is a likely auxiliary section.

Paper 2: LL(1) parsing in Dependent Lambek Calculus (with Max and Cass; target ~6–9 months). Characterize LL(1) parsers in DLC compositionally; derive a parser-generator algorithm from the characterization. Two critical claims from the 2026-04-22 meeting: recursive-descent parsers are unfolds, not folds, and the inverse of an initial algebra is always a recursive coalgebra (Cass's lever — verify against [alexandruIntrinsicallyCorrectAlgorithms2025-preprint] early). The derivative-based plan and its brzozowski-branch execution track supply the syntactic machinery (Brzozowski derivatives as the linear residual \multimap , decidable nullability, the amazing right adjoint). The regular-grammar precursor is deterministic regex → LL(1). Well-founded recursion is the recursion principle of record; guarded recursion ▷ / Löb, tracked at the well-founded-recursion milestone, remains as a fallback if Cass's lever does not transport to the substructural setting. Likely venue: POPL / ICFP / LICS.

Paper 3: Richer parsing classes and a usable Lean tool (target ~12–15 months). Generalize Paper 2's characterization to LL(k) and LR; fold in the Chu / GL-reduct treatment of parsers with structured failure (PEG, negative lookahead) via the recursive-coalgebra synthesis. The Lean port of the elaborator lands as a real tool — LinearElab already works for the linear core; the new development is the grammar-specific extensions and a parser-generation backend. Demonstrate on a non-trivial language fragment (an expression-language or JSON-class target). Likely venue: PLDI tools / ICFP / CPP.

Paper 4: Self-hosting parser correctness for Lean and Agda (target ~18–24 months; defense chapter). Encode the actual parser of Lean (resp. Agda) inside DLC, within Lean (resp. Agda) itself; prove correctness theorems against the language spec. This is the synthesis: it brings together Paper 1's metatheory, Papers 2–3's parsing characterizations, and Paper 3's implementation. Scope risk acknowledged — if lifting to both host languages overruns, narrow to one (Lean is the better-resourced bet given the existing LinearElab port). Likely venue: POPL / a top-tier journal / CPP / ITP.

Paper 5 (stretch): Transition-system verification by gluing. Apply the displayed-categorical-logic framework off-axis — glue over the free category of a distributed system's labelled transition system to extract safety / liveness proofs for mutex-class algorithms. Concrete and applications-flavored; slots in between any of Papers 2–4 if scheduling permits. Likely venue: CAV / CONCUR / verification.

html:p.html:strong: Side threads (not required for the PhD).

html:ul.html:li: DLC metatheorems via cubical-categorical-logic. Likely absorbed into the chapter for Paper 2 or Paper 4 as "we mechanize the following DLC metatheorems using our own logical-relations framework" rather than its own paper.
CBPV (or similar richer TT) metatheory. Eric Bond is working in this direction — collaboration opportunity, more naturally post-PhD or as a final-chapter sketch than a core chapter.
Locally-small / large category theory in Agda. Infrastructure for cubical-categorical-logic. Possible tools / library paper, but not a core chapter.
Practical transition-system verification. See Paper 5 above if it gets promoted from side thread.
Fuller 2-category library in Agda. Pure infrastructure; absorbed into the cubical-categorical-logic library where needed.
Displayed categories — under Paper 1 (logical relations) and Paper 4 (DLC metatheory).

Recursive coalgebras / well-founded recursion — under Papers 2–4. Cass's lever (Subterm ordering and the inverse of the initial algebra as a recursive coalgebra) is critical for Paper 2; verify early.

Strictification (Yoneda Strictification: Tradeoffs and Opportunities, Cayley strictification of grammars: StrictGrammar = Grammar → Grammar, Cayley strictification of a monoidal category, Fibrations into a 1-category of groupoid-object categories) — enabling tool for Papers 1 and 2 rather than a standalone paper, unless the methodology grows.
Lean implementation (How the LinearElab Elaborator Compiles to Category-Polymorphic Morphisms) — foundation for Papers 3 and 4; needs grammar-specific extensions beyond the current linear core.
Brzozowski derivatives + amazing right adjoint — concrete syntactic machinery for Paper 2, currently on the brzozowski worktree.
Guarded recursion ▷ / Löb (State and Attempt Löb Induction for ▷, ▷ as a Later Modality from Tiny Strings) — fallback recursion principle if the recursive-coalgebra story doesn't transport.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Pre-meeting agenda. Four items: (1) progress on logical relations, (2) progress on gluing, (3) an outline for a talk about the Logical Relations on Display work, (4) a sketch of the PhD roadmap. Follow-up to the 2026-05-05 meeting notes.

Logical relations — progress. Since last meeting the work on the paper has split along the two threads Max suggested. The conservativity-via-extensional-UMP fusion is still on the todo list for paper writing; the paper milestone gates the writing subtree on this. On the formalization side, the bottleneck is the slowness in Displayed.Instances.Sets.Properties — the benchmark investigation is now closed with a sharper cost model: under --lossy-unification, typing is ~1.3 percent of total cost; the remaining ~11.5s is post-typing bookkeeping over the unsolved-meta store, proportional to (\text {meta count}) \times (\text {per-meta type complexity}). Three independent levers: lossy (16×), explicit-refl on reind-filler⁻ (additional 2×), and strictification of the base (attacks per-meta type complexity, the largest residual factor).

Gluing — progress. The new piece since last meeting is the displayed-strictness / gluing-via-UMP pipeline: build the relevant vertical structure on YonedaStrictifyᴰ Cᴰ where displayed laws are refl; obtain a strict recursor F : \mathrm {Syn} \to \mathrm {YonedaStrictify}\,\mathcal {C} from the syntactic QIIT's UMP; reindex along F (strict because both base and displayed laws are refl, and the recursor maps identity and composition constructors to id and \cdot on the nose); apply the global elimination on the reindexed displayed category to get a section; transfer back through the round-trip natural iso at the boundary. The delicate observation is that displayed strictness is not implied by base strictness — YonedaStrictifyᴰ delivers it by composing displayed presheaf homomorphisms as functions, the same trick as the base. Open question to discuss: which gluing-in-the-library is the right first target, and how much of the existing Gluing/ infrastructure already lifts to the strictified setting versus needs duplication.

Talk outline — draft sections. Proposed shape, target ~45–60 minutes. (i) Motivation: mechanized metatheory and what displayed categories buy over total categories — keep examples small (canonicity, normalization). (ii) Setup: the displayed-categories framework over a cubical base, vertical structure, the key elimination principle. (iii) Main theorems: extensionality / fullness, the worked presented-categories example with equational axioms. (iv) Comparison: Twelf, Synthetic Tait Computability, Kaposi--Pujet. (v) Lessons from formalization: strictification trade-offs and the cost model from the slowness work. (vi) What's next: gluing, parser-side applications, parametric uses of displayed categories. Things to ask Max: target audience, which examples to actually work in slides, and whether (v) belongs in the talk or only in the paper.

PhD roadmap — sketch for discussion. See the expanded PhD-roadmap plan. Headline: DLC is the central object, developed along three coupled axes (semantics/metatheory via displayed categories, algorithmic content via parser characterizations, Lean implementation), with the synthesis chapter being self-hosted parser correctness for Lean and Agda. Four papers within the 24-month horizon (Paper 1 = the current one; Paper 2 = LL(1) in DLC with Max and Cass; Paper 3 = richer parsing classes + usable Lean tool; Paper 4 = self-hosting); a fifth stretch paper on transition-system verification by gluing; and side threads (CBPV with Eric Bond, 2-category library, large-category-theory infrastructure) explicitly out of scope.

fr:title.text: Benchmark cause of slowness in Displayed.Instances.Sets.Properties

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Benchmark cause of slowness in Displayed.Instances.Sets.Properties

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Build standalone Agda programs that measure typechecking time as a function of reindexing depth and proof style, to confirm or falsify the hypothesis that the slowness in Displayed.Instances.Sets.Properties comes from nested reindexings combined with filler-at-a-time proofs (many transports over refl).

Constraint: do not edit the library. The benchmarks should be contrived client programs that import existing library code and exercise the suspected-pathological patterns at controlled depth, so the measurement is attributable to a specific shape rather than the library as a whole. Compare against the hcomp-en-masse alternative from the hcomp speedup note.

Output: a short writeup of which patterns are linear-vs-superlinear in depth and which are not, sufficient to decide whether Yoneda strictification actually attacks the right cost. This decision gates the broader strictification experiments outlined in the 2026-05-05 meeting notes.
Background: the original slowness observation and the hcomp-based workaround. Subtask of the Logical Relations on Display milestone.
Bench files live at Bench/ReindFillerChains/. The driver is run-bench.sh; REPS=3 ./run-bench.sh reduces variance.

html:ul.html:li: Flat (Implicit/Explicit{01..32}.agda): Postulated Z, X : Type, pt : Z → X, q : (z : Z) → Yᴰ (pt z), with mp = refl ∙∙ refl ∙∙ refl and a chain rectifyOut $ reind-filler⁻ _ ∙ ... ∙ reind-filler⁻ _ of length n. The Explicit variants fill {a, b, p} on every reind-filler⁻.

Wrapped (Wrapped{01,04}.agda): Mirrors the actual goal shape — outer rectifyOut/reind-filler⁻/congᴰ around a funExt₂/ΣPathP that splits Zᴰ-side from Xᴰ-side, with the inner chain on the Xᴰ-side. mp is still refl ∙∙ refl ∙∙ refl; types are still postulated.

Real (Real{00,01,02,03,04,08,16,32,64}.agda and variants Real04NoLossy, Real04AllRefl, Real04AllReflNoLossy, RealFlat04): Faithful re-derivation of ExponentialsⱽSETᴰueⱽ.universalⱽ.snd.fst from Sets/Properties.agda — imports the real SETᴰ, Fibers, AllLRⱽSETᴰ, isFibrationSETᴰ, and varies inner-chain depth, the --lossy-unification flag, and whether each reind-filler⁻ takes _ or refl as its path argument. Real00 has no proof body (baseline for the import cost). RealFlat04 has the depth-4 ∙-chain but none of the rectifyOut/congᴰ/funExt₂/ΣPathP wrapping — it controls for the wrapping vs. the chain alone.

fr:title.text: What the bookkeeping is over: unsolved metas, not an elaborated term

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: What the bookkeeping is over: unsolved metas, not an elaborated term

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Removing --allow-unsolved-metas from Real04 fails with [UnsolvedConstraints]. Same for RealFlat04. So with --lossy-unification on, Agda doesn't actually finish elaborating the proof. The body persisted to the interface is a single reference to an unsolved meta (unsolvedmeta.N) parameterised by the module's level args. The "elaborated term" I attributed the cost to in earlier drafts of this tree doesn't exist.

What does exist in the meta-store: 384 unsolved metas for Real04, 174 for RealFlat04, 73 for Real00. Each unsolved meta carries a type, a context (telescope of variables in scope), and entries on Agda's constraint list. With lossy on, Agda gives up on the trickier ones rather than recursing forever, and they remain in the store. The 11.5s of bookkeeping is over those 384 meta entries, each of which has a SETᴰ.Hom[_][_,_]-flavoured type that mentions g*Xᴰ = isFibrationSETᴰ._*_ g Xᴰ, the cartesian-product-fibration combinator, LRⱽObᴰ→LRⱽ, etc.
Direct AST measurements on the postulated-type fixtures (which DO fully elaborate, no unsolved metas) — by reflection in Bench/ReindFillerChains/SizeReflect.agda:
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: GOAL ELABORATED AST NODES AGDA WALL TIME Implicit01 55 0.87s Implicit04 688 0.90s Implicit16 8,350 0.86s Implicit32 31,334 0.87s Wrapped01 688 0.97s Wrapped04 1,507 0.98s
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Two things stand out. First, on postulated types, term size grows quadratically with chain depth — 31k nodes at depth 32. Second, none of that matters for time: those cases all check in under 1s, dominated by interface-deserialization. So size alone is not the cost driver.

The cost driver is the meta store, not the elaborated term. Each Implicit/Wrapped AST node is R.def (quote postulate) — trivial for downstream passes to look up, highlight, serialize, and the postulated fixtures fully elaborate so no metas are left behind. In the real SETᴰ setting, the analogous pieces reference deep qualified names inside the displayed-presheaf infrastructure, the unifier under lossy gives up rather than recursing, and 384 entries remain in the meta store. The cost decomposes as
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: cost ≈ (meta count) × (per-meta type complexity) × (unifier work per call)
fr:mainmatter.html:p: where the "unifier work per call" factor is what --lossy-unification bounds at typing time, and the bookkeeping passes (InverseNameLookup, Highlighting, Serialization, Miscellaneous) walk the remaining (\text {meta count}) \times (\text {per-meta type complexity}) entries post-typing. Each lever attacks a different factor and they compose multiplicatively — see the annotation experiment below for the quantitative split.

The plateau on depth (Real04=13.0s, Real16=13.4s, Real32=14.1s, Real64=14.8s — ~30ms per junction past 4) is consistent: each extra junction adds one meta with similar type complexity, so the per-junction cost is small relative to the fixed cost of the wrapping itself.

fr:title.text: Why displayed presheaves are catastrophically worse

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Why displayed presheaves are catastrophically worse

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The same wrapping pattern, applied to displayed presheaves, has each junction's Hom-type be a NatTrans (component functions + naturality). Per-meta type complexity is multiplicatively bigger. Bookkeeping cost is (\text {meta count}) \times (\text {per-meta type complexity}), so the displayed-presheaf case scales worse along the type-complexity axis even at the same chain depth.

The comment in Sets/Properties.agda hypothesised that the slowness comes from "the unification of the implicit arguments to each of these reind fillers… we may mitigate the slowness here by removing nested reindexings." Sharper picture now:

html:ul.html:li: Right that unification is implicated and type-driven. 213s without --lossy-unification on the depth-4 chain; postulated-type fixtures (Wrapped, Implicit, Explicit) cannot reproduce the slowness even at depth 32 (31,334 AST nodes), so the cost is in unifying real SETᴰ.Hom[_][_,_] types, not in the chain shape itself.

Right that filling implicits helps — but the path argument, not the type implicits. Filling {a, b, p} on every reind-filler⁻ (the Explicit fixture) doesn't move the postulated case, which was already fast. But replacing the e : a ≡ b path argument with refl on the real chain gives a 2× speedup (13.13s → 6.20s on the bench, 14.83s → 6.75s in the actual library) by short-circuiting the unifier search at each reind-filler⁻ call.

Wrong about "nested reindexings" being the lever. Cutting nesting depth only saves ~30ms per junction past depth 4 — Real04≈Real16 ≈Real64 under lossy. The proof shape's chain length is not what's expensive.

The dominant residual cost is bookkeeping over the meta store. With lossy on, typing is 1.3 percent of the total; the remaining 11.5s is post-typing work over 384 unsolved metas, set by (\text {meta count}) \times (\text {per-meta type complexity}). Lossy and explicit-refl attack the typing factor; strictification is what attacks per-meta type complexity (and shrinks the bookkeeping bill proportionally).

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Yoneda strictification is still the right fix, with a sharper reason than the original comment suggested. The win is not "the unifier sees fewer reduction obligations". The win is "each unsolved meta in the store has a smaller, simpler type", because the strictified fiber types substituted into each junction are smaller. The downstream bookkeeping passes (scope lookup, highlighting, interface build) walk those meta types and shrink proportionally.

Concrete prediction: strictification should drop Real04 from ~13s back toward Real00's ~3.4s import baseline, mostly by collapsing the Miscellaneous + InverseNameLookup + Highlighting + Serialization buckets, not the Typing bucket (which is already small under lossy).

It will not eliminate the import cost (Real00 is 3.4s with the current import graph, almost entirely in deserialization) — that's a separate concern about the size of the displayed-presheaf infrastructure being pulled in.

It does not obviate --lossy-unification: removing lossy turns the depth-4 case into 213s. The three levers attack different factors of (meta count) × (per-meta type complexity) × (unifier work per call) and are independent:

html:ul.html:li: --lossy-unification bounds unifier work per call (16×).
_ → refl annotation further cuts unifier work per call on top of lossy (2× more).
Strictification shrinks per-meta type complexity, which feeds through to both the typing cost and the post-typing bookkeeping.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: All three should be applied together. Strictification is the most invasive but addresses the largest single multiplier and the only one that touches the bookkeeping bill.

fr:mainmatter.html:pre: Properties.agda (Exp commented out) 3.79 s Properties.agda (Exp live, `_` × 6) 14.83 s Properties.agda (Exp live, refl × 6) 6.75 s
fr:mainmatter.html:p: 2.18× speedup in the real file. The bench was faithful — the same change that worked on the contrived bench works on the actual definition. Caveat: the _s in isFibrationSETᴰueⱽ and BinProductsⱽSETᴰueⱽ do not accept refl (those fillers produce non-trivial paths, unlike the rectifyOut/congᴰ-wrapped chain inside Exp). The intervention is specific to wrapped reindexing chains.

html:ul.html:li: Lossy attacks per-meta type complexity. It bounds how much work the unifier does normalizing the huge SETᴰ.Hom[_][_,_] types attached to each meta.

Annotation attacks per-meta unifier work. Even after lossy makes each meta tractable, the unifier still spends real time searching for e : a ≡ b at each reind-filler⁻ call. Handing it refl short-circuits that search.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Meta count is essentially unchanged (384 → 389, basically noise). The user's hypothesis that "filling earlier metas resolves later ones" is not what's happening — invisible metas like _b_237, _a_276, _bᴰ.fst_358 survive both runs. Annotation reduces work per meta, not number of metas.
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: cost ≈ (meta count) × (per-meta type complexity) × (unifier work per call) ↑ ↑ ↑ (mostly fixed (lossy attacks (annotation attacks by proof shape) this; strictifi- this) cation also)
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Practical take: in real Properties.agda code, the easy mechanical intervention reind-filler⁻ _ → reind-filler⁻ refl (where applicable) should give about a 2× speedup. It does not obviate --lossy-unification or strictification — those still own the bigger factors.

This explains the user's prior empirical observation: running C-u C-u C-c C-s (Solve constraints at strongest normalization) on ? holes returns refl-shaped solutions that, when written back into the source, give exactly this 2× speedup. The investigation here just quantifies what that interactive workflow was achieving.

Caveat: writing refl only works because, in this specific proof shape, every e : a ≡ b arising from reind-filler⁻ reduces under the rectifyOut/congᴰ wrapping to a path of compositions that collapses to refl once the implicit fiber types are pinned. In a more general chain you might need a non-trivial composite — but in that case C-u C-u C-c C-s still gives the right thing.

Decision implication: strictification + lossy + explicit refl are the three independent levers. Strictification is the most invasive but addresses the largest factor (per-meta type complexity, multiplicatively shrinks meta sizes); the _→refl cleanup is a cheap mechanical 2× before doing any structural work.

html:ul.html:li: The depth 3→4 step (Real03 = 4.07s, Real04 = 12.97s) is now understood as "first successful elaboration", not a lossy threshold. Real01–Real03 fail fast with a type-mismatch error because the chain is too short for endpoints to unify. Depth 4 is the minimum chain length that elaborates at all, at which point the post-typing bookkeeping fires. Worth confirming by a typecheck-only benchmark that disables Highlighting and Serialization, if Agda exposes the knobs.

Does the refl-annotation lever transfer to the UniversalQuantifierⱽ proof shape? ExponentialsⱽSETᴰueⱽ benefits 2× because its rectifyOut/congᴰ-wrapped chain reduces to refl once implicits are pinned. The non-Eq UQ counterpart isn't written in the library yet (the legacy commented block in Sets/Properties.agda uses an obsolete API). When someone is already inside that file, attempting the construction is the cheapest way to find out.

Does the snd .snd field (currently a {!!} hole in ExponentialsⱽSETᴰueⱽ and in the bench files) have the same shape when filled? It would add another rectifyOut/congᴰ/funExt₂/ΣPathP block and (per the cost model) multiply the meta count again.

Is Scoping.InverseNameLookup actually triggered by typing-time pretty-printing of constraints, in which case it's partly typing cost masquerading as bookkeeping? Highlighting and Serialization (3.76s combined) are unambiguously post-typing; the Miscellaneous + InverseNameLookup attribution is fuzzier. The qualitative claim ("typing under lossy is a small slice, meta-store bookkeeping dominates") holds either way.

fr:title.text: Meeting with Max 2026-05-05: strictification, conservativity, slowness

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Meeting with Max 2026-05-05: strictification, conservativity, slowness

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Notes from a meeting with Max about strictification, wrapping up conservativity for the Logical Relations on Display paper, and chasing the source of slowness in Displayed.Instances.Sets.Properties.

Three layers of strictification are now on the table. The ExtraId category buys judgmental \mathrm {IdL} for free. A Yoneda strictification of the base — taking morphisms to be PshHomStrict between representables — promotes both unitors and associativity to refl. Pushing the same trick one level up, by replacing the elements of a presheaf P with PshHomStrict from the Yoneda embedding into P, makes F-id and F-seq of every presheaf definitional too.

Open question: what survives the strictification? The library's existing constructions and logical relations live over the non-strict base. We need to articulate how the strictified versions relate back — i.e., how the same logical relations are extracted from a proof done over the strict side. This is the same boundary cost flagged in the Yoneda strictification tradeoffs note; the answer is what determines whether strictification is worth integrating versus running as a private experiment.

Conservativity for the paper. The current presented-lambda conservativity proof is split across two steps; Max suggests fusing them by proving fullness through an extensional universal property directly. If the strictification experiments work out, including them gives a more direct comparison to Kaposi--Pujet and corroborates their strictification observations.

Plan for the strictification experiments. (i) Identify the minimal amount of library code that would need to be duplicated or rewritten over a strict base. (ii) Verify the vector of slowness — strictification only helps if the cost actually lives in unitor/associator reindexing. (iii) Build the strict version, conditional on (i) and (ii) being favorable.

Slowness measurement. The slowness is concentrated in Displayed.Instances.Sets.Properties: vertical exponentials and the universal quantifier over the displayed sets category typecheck pathologically slowly despite simple goals. Working hypothesis (consistent with the slow filler chains note and the hcomp speedup note): the cost is the depth of nested reindexings combined with the filler-at-a-time proof style, where many of the offending transports are over refl. Tracked separately as a benchmark TODO — gates the broader strictification decision.

fr:title.text: Fibrations into a 1-category of groupoid-object categories

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Fibrations into a 1-category of groupoid-object categories

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Explore a streamlined setup for logical relations: work with a small category \mathcal {GC} whose objects are categories equipped with a groupoid object (or, equivalently, categories in which every map is invertible in the relevant sense), and whose morphisms are the appropriate structure-preserving functors. Define fibrations as functors into \mathcal {GC}. Because each fiber is a groupoid-enriched 1-category, \mathcal {GC} itself is a 1-category — there are no higher coherences to manage.

Motivation. The current displayed-category machinery in Finishing Logical Relations on Display spends a lot of effort on coherences that evaporate once the fibers are forced to be (truncated to) groupoidal. If the target 1-category is rich enough to express the constructions needed for canonicity and normalization logical relations, this may be a lighter foundation than the thickened / displayed-double-category route.

html:ol.html:li: Define the small 1-category \mathcal {GC} of categories-with-groupoid-objects and verify it is a 1-category (no higher cells).
Define fibrations as functors E \to \mathcal {GC} and relate them to the displayed-category presentation already in the library.
Encode the universal properties needed for semantics: terminal / binary products / exponentials at the base, plus their fiberwise analogues.
Encode universal quantification (right adjoint to pullback / reindexing) internally to this framework.
State and prove Beck--Chevalley for the relevant pullback squares.
State and prove Frobenius reciprocity for the left-adjoint / existential direction.
Reconstruct the canonicity logical relation in this framework as a first test case.
Reconstruct the normalization logical relation in this framework as a harder stress test.

html:ul.html:li: What exactly is the right notion of "groupoid object" here — an internal groupoid, a hom-groupoid enrichment, or truncation of hom-sets to sets? The choice affects whether \mathcal {GC} is genuinely small.
Does the 1-categorical structure survive once we add the universal-quantifier / Beck--Chevalley / Frobenius data, or do higher coherences creep back in through the adjoints?
How does this compare to the displayed-category-with-isos setup in Cubical/Categories/Displayed/ and the thickened displayed categories of PR 253?

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The first bulk push from forester-apple-sync crashed on this very tree. That would also fix any other tree that mentions meta or tag declarations in its body.

Defensive secondary fix (also not done). forester-org--push-reminder could catch the Invalid index osascript error on the update path and fall back to creating a fresh reminder. Useful regardless of the parser fix, since stale apple-ids can also arise from the user manually deleting reminders.
